Both protocol surfaces in `src/kailash/trust/` are pinned to specification
revisions that have since been superseded, and in both cases the upstream
projects now publish an official conformance suite we could be scoring against.
Filing so the drift is tracked rather than discovered by an integrator.

## 1. MCP — two revisions behind, and the newer one is architectural

`src/kailash/trust/mcp/server.py:74`

```python
_SUPPORTED_MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS = ("2025-06-18", "2025-03-26", "2024-11-05")
```

The current revision is **`2026-07-28`**. Revisions published on
<https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/>, in order: `2024-11-05`,
`2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25`, `2026-07-28`. So our newest supported
version is two releases behind.

This is not a matter of adding a few methods. Quoting
<https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning>:

> There is no negotiation handshake. Every request carries its protocol version,
> and the server accepts or rejects each request independently.

and its terminology section distinguishes **Modern** (`2026-07-28` and later,
per-request metadata) from **Legacy** (`2025-11-25` and earlier, `initialize`
handshake). The spec's own compatibility matrix rates *Modern client / Legacy
server* as **"Fails."** A client that has dropped legacy support cannot talk to a
server built around `initialize` at all.

The changelog for that revision also removes `ping`, `logging/setLevel` and
`notifications/roots/list_changed`, adds a `server/discover` RPC that servers
**MUST** implement, and adds a required `resultType` on every result.

### There is an official conformance suite

`github.com/modelcontextprotocol/conformance`, published to npm as
`@modelcontextprotocol/conformance`. Worth wiring into CI so the number is
measured rather than asserted.

One caveat worth knowing before anyone quotes a score: the **stable** release
(`0.1.16`) cannot target the latest revision —

```
$ npx @modelcontextprotocol/conformance@0.1.16 list --server --spec-version 2026-07-28
Unknown spec version: 2026-07-28
Valid versions: 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, draft, extension
```

`2026-07-28` scoring lives only in the `alpha` dist-tag (`0.2.0-alpha.11`), which
is also where the frozen per-revision requirement sets are. Note there is **no**
`requirements/2025-06-18.yaml`, so the revision we currently declare has no
frozen requirement set at all — any conformance claim needs to name the tool
version that produced it.

Per-revision JSON Schemas are published under
`schema/<revision>/schema.json` in the specification repo and make a good
machine oracle for serialization, independent of the suite.

## 2. A2A — the agent-card well-known path was renamed

`src/kailash/trust/a2a/service.py:175`

```python
@app.endpoint("/.well-known/agent.json", methods=["GET"])
```

`/.well-known/agent.json` is the **0.2.x** location. Current revisions serve the
card at **`/.well-known/agent-card.json`**. Tags published at
`api.github.com/repos/a2aproject/A2A/tags`: `v1.0.1`, `v1.0.0`, `v1.0.0-rc`,
`v0.3.0`, `v0.2.6` … — so 0.2.x is several releases back.

A grep over `src/kailash/trust/a2a/` finds no matches for `message/send`,
`tasks/get`, `agent-card.json`, or the 1.0 PascalCase method names, against a
positive control confirming the pattern machinery works on that tree. So the
JSON-RPC layer present in `jsonrpc.py` does not currently carry the specified
method set.

### There is an official TCK

`github.com/a2aproject/a2a-tck` (Apache-2.0). It fetches the card from the
well-known path, drives every interface the card declares, and emits
`compatibility.json` plus JUnit XML, graded RFC 2119 (MUST = hard failure). Its
`specification/version.json` pins the exact spec commit it tests, which makes it
a better citation than a docs banner.

Two things to decide before adopting it:

- **Which version line to target.** `v1.0` has a stable TCK pinned to a released
  spec commit. The `0.3` line's TCK is a beta (`0.3.0.beta5`) whose spec baseline
  is a snapshot of `main` taken before `v0.3.0` was tagged — so "passes the 0.3
  TCK" and "conforms to released 0.3.0" are adjacent claims, not the same one.
- **The suite is not purely black-box.** Per its `docs/SUT_REQUIREMENTS.md`, the
  system under test must recognise a set of `messageId` prefixes that link tests
  to expected behaviour, so a test-only mode is needed.

## 3. Suggested disposition

1. Decide and record a target revision for each protocol, with the reason.
   Pinning deliberately is fine; pinning by omission is what this issue is about.
2. Wire the official suites into CI so the score is a measured artifact.
3. Gate on **per-requirement success by name**, not on absence of failures — both
   suites skip capability-gated tests, and a skip and a pass are the same colour
   to a failure-counting gate.
4. Derive the A2A agent card from mounted routes rather than hand-writing it.
   Declaring a capability that is not implemented turns skips into hard failures.

## 4. One thing not to do

The A2A TCK writes a `compliance_badge` string into its own output. That badge is
generated by running the tool against your own endpoint and is conferred by
nobody. It should never appear in documentation or marketing as an award.
","comments":[{"id":"IC_kwDORmHuac8AAAABP7YTQA","author":{"login":"esperie"},"authorAssociation":"MEMBER","body":"## DECISION — D-A, D-B, D-C ratified (co-owner, 2026-08-21)

Recording the co-owner's ratification in this session so the target revisions are durable and this issue is no longer blocked. All three were ratified as recommended in the cont-22 sweep report § 5.

### D-A — MCP target revision: **Modern (`2026-07-28`)**

Not Legacy-latest (`2025-11-25`). Rationale as recommended: the spec's own compatibility matrix rates Modern client → Legacy server as **"Fails"**, so Legacy-latest buys currency without buying interop — one revision forward and still unable to talk to a client that dropped legacy support. Modern is the only option that reaches conformance rather than deferring it.

**This is an architecture change, not a version bump.** Measured against `src/kailash/trust/mcp/` on main:

```
server/discover   -> 0    (a MUST in 2026-07-28)
resultType        -> 0    (required on every result in 2026-07-28)
initialize        -> 21   (the Legacy handshake the Modern revision removes)
ping              -> 5    (removed in 2026-07-28)
```

`server.py:74` declares `("2025-06-18", "2025-03-26", "2024-11-05")`. The server is Legacy by construction. Estimated 2–4 autonomous cycles; MUST be sharded per `autonomous-execution.md` § Per-Session Capacity Budget rather than attempted in one pass.

### D-B — A2A target line: **1.0**

Not 0.3. Rationale as recommended: 1.0's TCK is pinned to a released spec commit, so "passes the TCK" and "conforms to the release" are the same claim. The 0.3 TCK is beta (`0.3.0.beta5`) against a spec baseline snapshotted from `main` before `v0.3.0` was tagged — the two claims come apart, and a green run would not mean what it appears to. Accepted con: 1.0 is the larger jump from our 0.2.x surface.

**Scope correction to this issue's original text:** the well-known path appears in **four** files, not the single `service.py:175` cited — also `service.py:11` (docstring), `models.py:84`, `agent_card.py:209`. A rename touches all four. The 1.0 method set is absent (`message/send`, `tasks/get`, `agent-card.json`, `SendMessage`, `GetTask` all 0 hits, against a `jsonrpc` → 23 control confirming the grep works on that tree).

### D-C — TCK non-black-box requirement: **env-gated, fail-closed, security-reviewed**

The TCK's `SUT_REQUIREMENTS.md` needs the system under test to recognise `messageId` prefixes — test-only behaviour in production code. Gate it behind an env flag that defaults **OFF** and **fails closed**, and review it as a security surface rather than test scaffolding. It is production code that changes behaviour on attacker-influenceable input, so it carries the same bar as any other trust boundary (`security.md` § Secure-Default For A New Security Feature).

### Binding constraint on both conformance suites

Per the sweep report's recommendation 2, which stands: **wire both suites into CI gated per-requirement by name, not on absence of failures.** Both suites skip capability-gated tests, and to a failure-counting gate a skip and a pass are the same colour. Also standing: **do not quote the A2A `compliance_badge`** — it is emitted by running the tool against your own endpoint and is conferred by nobody.

### Status

Unblocked for planning. Next step is a sharded wave plan (`/todos`), which carries its own human approval gate — implementation does not begin on this comment alone.

Root cause was a **test mock that had drifted from the contract it stands in for**:

```
production:  verify(agent_id, "trust_verify", level=level)
real API:    verify(agent_id, action, resource=None, level=STANDARD, context=None)
test mock:   mock_verify(agent_id, level=None)          <- omits `action`
```

So `"trust_verify"` bound to `level` positionally *and* `level=` was passed again → `TypeError` → JSON-RPC `-32603 Internal error`.

The handler matches the real signature. **The mock was fixed, not the production call** — changing the handler to satisfy a wrong mock would have broken the real API to make a fiction pass. Swept the sibling mocks in the same fixture (`mock_get_chain`, `mock_get_public_key`): both still match. One drifted, not a class.

`37 passed` (was 33 passed / 4 failed). Wider `tests/trust/`: `6366 passed, 33 skipped`.

### Still open on Wave 1

**W1B** — the 1.0 method set. Re-derived and still entirely absent: `message/send`, `tasks/get`, `SendMessage`, `GetTask` all return 0 hits, against a control (`jsonrpc` → 23) confirming the grep works on that tree. The current registered set is 0.2.x-shaped dot-notation: `agent.capabilities`, `agent.invoke`, `trust.verify`, `trust.delegate`, `audit.query`.

Wave 1 Shard B is done and in `dev` (`6e4e652da`). The agent now registers the
A2A 1.0 JSON-RPC methods **`SendMessage`** and **`GetTask`**.

### The plan named two protocol generations as one method set

The approved wave plan's 1B row read: *"The 1.0 method set: `message/send`,
`tasks/get`, `SendMessage`, `GetTask`."* Those are **not** one method set. Measured
against `a2aproject/A2A` at tag `v1.0.1` before implementing:

`docs/specification.md` § "Protocol Requirements":

> **Method Naming:** PascalCase method names matching gRPC conventions (e.g.,
> `SendMessage`, `GetTask`)

§ "Method Mapping Reference" splits the columns explicitly:

| Functionality | JSON-RPC Method | REST Endpoint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Send message | `SendMessage` | `POST /message:send` |
| Get task | `GetTask` | `GET /tasks/{id}` |

All eight § 9.4 method sections use PascalCase. So `message/send` / `tasks/get` are
the **0.2.x/0.3.x** JSON-RPC names; `/message:send` and `/tasks/{id}` are 1.0's
**REST** endpoints. Neither is a 1.0 JSON-RPC method name.

Registering the slash spellings would have advertised 1.0 conformance the 1.0 TCK
then fails — the precise outcome D-B was ratified to avoid, since 1.0's TCK is
pinned to a released spec commit. A regression test now asserts those names are
**not** registered, so a future "fix" back toward the plan's wording reds the suite
rather than shipping.

**This issue's own text is consistent with the correction** — it greps for
"`message/send`, `tasks/get`, `agent-card.json`, or the 1.0 PascalCase method
names" as things *absent*, which already treats PascalCase as the 1.0 set. The
error was the plan transcribing that absent-list as the target list.

### Scope: v1.0 has 11 JSON-RPC methods, not 2

W1B delivered the 2 the plan budgeted for. The other **9** are real, un-planned
surface and are now tracked as **shard 1C** rather than absorbed or dropped:
`SendStreamingMessage`, `ListTasks`, `CancelTask`, `SubscribeToTask`,
`GetExtendedAgentCard`, and the four `*TaskPushNotificationConfig` methods. Two are
streaming (SSE) — a different transport concern from W1B's request/response pair —
so 1C is likely ≥2 shards and should be sized at `/todos`, not treated as a tail of
1B.

### The data model was a hidden prerequisite

`SendMessage`/`GetTask` are unimplementable without the v1.0 core types, which the
plan did not anticipate: `Role`, `TaskState`, `Part`, `Message`, `Artifact`,
`TaskStatus`, `Task`. Note `Part` is a **`oneof`** in 1.0 (text/raw/url/data in one
type), replacing 0.2.x's separate `TextPart`/`FilePart`/`DataPart`.

Three wire conventions are spec MUSTs and are pinned by tests rather than left to
preference:

- **camelCase** field names — § "JSON Serialization": *"All JSON serializations of
  the A2A protocol data model MUST use camelCase naming for field names, not the
  snake_case convention used in Protocol Buffer definitions."*
- **ProtoJSON enum values** — `TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED`, not an ordinal or a lowercased alias.
- **`TaskNotFoundError` → `-32001`** per § "Error Code Mappings". A generic `-32602`
  would be indistinguishable to a conformant client from a malformed request.

### Two pre-existing defects fixed on the way

- `jsonrpc.py` carried two `except Exception: pass` blocks that silently swallowed
  failures while enriching an already-decided verdict. Both now log and degrade
  explicitly.
- `service.py` attached lifecycle handlers via `fastapi_app.on_event`. Nexus's own
  `add_startup_handler` docstring names this as a trap — the property returns `None`
  until `register()`/`start()` triggers lazy gateway init, so the registration
  silently depended on call order. Routed through Nexus, which owns the lifespan.
  Side effect: the A2A suite went from **52 warnings to 0**.

### Verification

19 new tests pass. Because a green suite is not by itself evidence, four mutations
were run to show it discriminates — each reddened, each with a probe confirming the
mutation reached the code:

| mutation | result |
| --- | --- |
| also register `message/send` + `tasks/get` | 2 failed |
| emit `context_id` instead of `contextId` | 1 failed |
| renumber `TaskNotFoundError` to `-32602` | 2 failed |
| drop the terminal-task guard | 1 failed |

kaizen A2A integration suite: 37 passed, 0 warnings.

**Still open on this issue:** Wave 2 (MCP → Modern `2026-07-28`, 4 shards,
architectural), Wave 3 (conformance gating), and now Wave 1C.

Measured, with a control (a `grep` that returns 0 everywhere proves nothing unless it is shown to fire here):

```
git merge-base --is-ancestor 6e4e652da HEAD   -> ancestor (W1B IS in history)

git grep -c SendMessage HEAD       -- 'src/**/*.py'  -> empty
```

`src/kailash/trust/a2a/messaging.py` and `task_store.py` are ABSENT at HEAD. Removed by:

```
93323218e revert(a2a,2203): pull W1B from the trunk -- introduced cross-agent task read/write
```

The revert is correct and well-argued — an adversarial review executed two end-to-end attacks against what W1B added (`GetTask` with no ownership predicate returning another agent's message history; `SendMessage` honouring a client-supplied `taskId` against an existing task, a confused-deputy into the victim's context). It reverted rather than patching because a correct ownership check needs a caller identity that did not exist at the time.

### That blocker is now GONE, which changes W1B's disposition

The revert recorded the pre-existing hole it could not build on: `A2AAuthenticator.verify_token` had no call site in the request path, so `handle()` tested the bearer token for truthiness and discarded it. **That has since been fixed**, in four commits after the revert:

```
35fc66f01 fix(a2a,2203)!: verify bearer tokens; hand handlers an identity, not a string
191fb8db8 fix(a2a,2203)!: close the response-cache auth bypass and the audience no-op
7fe9b6ad8 fix(a2a,2203)!: remove the allow_unverified_tokens escape hatch
d6e4bf90d feat(a2a,2203)!: authorize protected methods through PACT, fail-closed
```

At HEAD, `jsonrpc.py:225` calls `verify_token`, re-asserts the audience independently of the verifier, refuses when no verifier or no `expected_audience` is configured, and returns a `CallerIdentity`. So the identity the revert said W1B needed and lacked now exists.

**W1B is therefore re-landable**, and should be re-scoped rather than treated as done: re-implement `SendMessage`/`GetTask` with an ownership predicate bound to `CallerIdentity.agent_id`, and a server-derived `role` rather than the client-supplied one the revert flagged as forgeable.

### The spec correction W1B produced still stands

A2A 1.0 JSON-RPC method names are PascalCase; `message/send` / `tasks/get` are the 0.2.x/0.3.x names and `/message:send` / `/tasks/{id}` are 1.0's REST endpoints. Unaffected by the revert.

| --- | --- |
| `_SUPPORTED_MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS` | `("2025-06-18", "2025-03-26", "2024-11-05")` — `server.py:74`, line number still accurate |
| `server/discover` (a 2026-07-28 MUST) | 0 |
| `resultType` (required on every result) | 0 |
| `initialize` (the handshake Modern removes) | 21 |
| `ping` (removed in 2026-07-28) | 5 |
| A2A well-known path | `agent-card.json` at 3 sites in `src/kailash/trust/a2a/`; the 0.2.x spelling survives only in `CHANGELOG.md`, correctly (historical record) |
| A2A 1.0 JSON-RPC methods registered | 0 of 11 |

So W1A holds; W1B is open again; W1C (9 methods) and Wave 2 (MCP → Modern) are untouched.

### Suggested bookkeeping

Re-open W1B as a shard with the ownership requirement written into its acceptance criteria, so the re-land cannot repeat the defect the revert caught. Per #2189's shape 6, a correction that lives only in a commit message is a deferral with no reader — which is why it is recorded here.

Filing here because this repo is `coc-build` and the durable upflow for a COC-tooling defect is a `/codify` proposal ingested at loom Gate-1 — loom splits, it does not originate (`artifact-flow.md`). See § Routing at the end.

## Summary

The CLI emitter writes a **dotless staging layout** by design. Gate-2 copied that staging tree into the target worktree **without applying the staging→installed path mapping**, so `codex/` and `gemini/` landed at the repo root next to the untouched `.codex/` and `.gemini/` trees.

The emitter is not the bug. The delivery step is.

## Evidence that the dotless layout is intentional — in the emitter

`emit-cli-artifacts.mjs` header, verbatim:

```
 * Output layout (with --out <dir>):
 *
 *   <dir>/codex/
 *     prompts/<cmd>.md                    one per non-excluded .claude/commands/<cmd>.md
 *     skills/<nn-name>/SKILL.md
 *
 *   <dir>/gemini/
 *     commands/<cmd>.toml     one per non-excluded command (TOML per Gemini spec)
 *     skills/<nn-name>/SKILL.md
 *     agents/<name>.md
```

and the implementation agrees:

```
emit-cli-artifacts.mjs:209   const codexPath  = path.join(outDir, "codex", "prompts", `${codexName}.md`);
emit-cli-artifacts.mjs:227   const geminiPath = path.join(outDir, "gemini", "commands", `${geminiName}.toml`);
emit-cli-artifacts.mjs:339   const skillOut   = path.join(outDir, cli, "skills", skill);
emit-cli-artifacts.mjs:1026  const outPath    = path.join(outDir, "codex", "prompts", `${promptName}.md`);
emit-cli-artifacts.mjs:1089  const outPath    = path.join(outDir, "gemini", "agents", `${name}.md`);
```

**These lines are unchanged in this sync** — `git diff <base>...<PR> -- .claude/bin/emit-cli-artifacts.mjs` matching `(join|resolve)\(.*(codex|gemini)` is empty. The emitter behaved exactly as it always has.

The same file refers to the *delivered* locations with the dot throughout (`.codex/prompts/`, `.codex/hooks.json`, `.gemini/settings.json`), so the two-form distinction is deliberate: **dotless = staging under `--out`, dotted = installed at repo root.**

## The validator encodes the same two-root distinction

```
validate-emit.mjs:1071   const gCmdDir    = join(emitDir, "gemini",  "commands");   # EMIT root  → dotless
validate-emit.mjs:1090   const cPromptDir = join(emitDir, "codex",   "prompts");    # EMIT root  → dotless
validate-emit.mjs:1224   ["installed:.codex/skills",  join(root, ".codex",  "skills")]   # REPO root → dotted
validate-emit.mjs:1225   ["installed:.gemini/skills", join(root, ".gemini", "skills")]   # REPO root → dotted
```

Two roots, two forms, by design. Gate-2 wrote the emit-root form to the repo root.

## What landed

```
  PR:.codex  -> 476 files      main:.codex  -> 476
  PR:codex   -> 475 files      main:codex   ->   0
  PR:.gemini -> 475 files      main:.gemini -> 475
  PR:gemini  -> 475 files      main:gemini  ->   0
```

All 950 dotless entries are status `A`; `.codex/`/`.gemini/` are not touched at all. Not a rename — the PR's own manifest reports `+1423 ~111 -4`, four deletions total.

Classifying each dotless file against its dotted twin on `main`:

```
dotless files added: 950
  identical to dotted twin (pure duplicate):   912
  dotted twin exists, CONTENT DIFFERS:          36
  no dotted twin (genuinely new):                2
```

The 912 are bloat. **The 36 + 2 are the failure**: those updates sit at a path no CLI loads while the live dotted artifact stays stale — a delivery that reports success and delivers nothing. The two new ones are `codex/skills/wrapup/SKILL.md` and `gemini/skills/wrapup/SKILL.md`, which would be absent from the installed trees entirely.

## It regressed — the previous sync was correct

`git show 49514e8a3 --stat` (PR #2123, loom `dc07a7c6cc4d`, 2026-08-13) delivered to `.codex/prompts`, `.codex/skills`, `.gemini/agents`, `.gemini/commands`, `.gemini/skills` — all dotted. So the mapping existed and worked six days earlier.

## Where the defect is — and why I cannot cite the line

The Gate-2 engine is loom-side and is **not** distributed to this repo:

```
.claude/bin/sync-tier-aware.mjs      absent
.claude/bin/sync-gate2-worktree.mjs  absent
.claude/bin/coc-sync.mjs             absent
(control) .claude/bin/emit-cli-artifacts.mjs  PRESENT
```

So the failing line is in one of those, and I can characterize the defect but not point at it. Per `artifact-flow.md` the engine is `sync-tier-aware.mjs` invoked with `--out <worktree>` by `sync-gate2-worktree.mjs`; the mapping that appears to have been dropped is the one `coc-sync` Step 6.6 documents for the sibling case (`.codex/hooks.json` + `.gemini/settings.json` copied from `codex-templates/` + `gemini-templates/`).

**The most likely shape:** the emit staging dir and the worktree out-dir were unified onto one `--out`, so the emitter's dotless staging tree became the delivered tree. That would explain why the CC (`.claude/`) and `.coc/` lanes are unaffected — those two lanes carry their dot in the source path, so no mapping is needed for them, and only the CLI lanes rely on the staging→installed translation.

## Suggested acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gate-2 delivers CLI artifacts to `.codex/**` and `.gemini/**`; a distribution run produces zero files at top-level `codex/` or `gemini/`.
- [ ] A regression check asserts the invariant directly — after a Gate-2 run against a scratch worktree, `git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD -- codex gemini` is empty while `.codex`/`.gemini` are non-empty. (Asserting only that `.codex` is non-empty does not discriminate: it was non-empty *before* this sync too, which is exactly why the regression shipped green.)
- [ ] The 38 artifacts this sync failed to deliver (36 changed + 2 new) land at their installed paths on re-emit.

## What

`packages/kailash-pact/src/pact/governance/api/endpoints.py` — every write endpoint binds an authenticated `identity`, and not one uses it as the actor. The actor is taken from the request body instead.

`POST /clearances` (endpoints.py:304-345):

```python
async def grant_clearance(
    request: Request,
    req: GrantClearanceRequest,
    identity: str = Depends(auth.require_write),      # bound, never read
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    clearance = RoleClearance(
        role_address=resolved_address,
        max_clearance=ConfidentialityLevel(req.max_clearance),
        granted_by_role_address=req.granted_by_role_address,   # <-- from the body
        vetting_status=VettingStatus.ACTIVE,
    )
    ...
    await emit_governance_event(
        GovernanceEventType.CLEARANCE_GRANTED,
        {..., "granted_by": req.granted_by_role_address},
        source_role_address=req.granted_by_role_address,       # <-- and into the audit event
    )
```

`GrantClearanceRequest.validate_granted_by` (schemas.py:232-236) validates only that the string is a well-formed D/T/R address. Nothing compares it to the caller.

Sibling, same shape, same file: `POST /knowledge-share-policies` sets `created_by_role_address=req.created_by_role_address`.

The value is durable on both surfaces — it is written into the stored `RoleClearance` and into the governance audit event as `source_role_address`. `pact/examples/university/clearance.py` shows `D1-R1` used as the self-granting root authority, so the address a caller would want to claim is discoverable from the shipped examples.

## Why it is not a one-line fix

`security.md` § Enforcement-Surface Parity → "Identity-derivation parity" says the actor must be server-derived from the authenticated session. **There is nothing to derive it from.** `GovernanceAuth.verify_token` (auth.py:75-106) compares one shared bearer token and returns a constant:

```python
if hmac.compare_digest(token, self._api_token):
    return "authenticated"
```

Every authenticated caller is the same principal. `identity` is `"authenticated"` or `"anonymous"` — never a role address. So `granted_by_role_address == identity` cannot be written, and rejecting the body field outright would break the only way the field is currently populated.

Grep confirms the gap is uniform, not an oversight at one endpoint: `identity` is bound at all nine endpoints (lines 109, 164, 209, 242, 281, 308, 355, 401, 456) and read at none.

## The decision needed

Which of these is the intended model?

1. **Per-principal tokens.** Tokens carry a role address; `identity` becomes that address; body actor fields are dropped and derived server-side. Correct, and the largest change — it touches token issuance, not just these endpoints.
2. **Caller-asserted but labelled.** Keep the body field, but record it as an unverified claim (`granted_by_claimed`), so an auditor reading the record cannot mistake an assertion for an authenticated fact. Cheap, honest, and does not pretend to an authorization property.
3. **Authorize the assertion.** Keep the field, but require the token's scope to cover the claimed grantor address — needs a token→address mapping, i.e. most of option 1.

Until one is chosen, the record says a role granted a clearance when what actually happened is that somebody holding the shared token said so.

## Scope note

Not exploitable as a *privilege* escalation on its own — `require_write` still gates the call, so an unauthenticated caller cannot reach it. The defect is in the **provenance**: the clearance record and the governance audit event both name a grantor that the system never verified acted.","comments":[{"id":"IC_kwDORmHuac8AAAABUISBvA","author":{"login":"esperie"},"authorAssociation":"MEMBER","body":"## Re-derivation of every load-bearing claim, and a PARTIAL fix that does not pre-empt the decision

The issue's disposition was right: options 1 and 3 are authorization-schema decisions and I have not implemented either. What I did implement is option 2 — and only after measuring three things that could have killed it. Every claim below was re-derived with my own command, not read off the issue.

### Claims CONFIRMED

| Claim | Instrument | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `identity` bound at 9 endpoints, read at none | `grep -n "identity" endpoints.py` | exactly 9 hits, all `Depends(...)` bindings, at **109, 164, 209, 242, 281, 308, 355, 401, 456** — the issue's line numbers were exact, not stale |
| Body-sourced actor at 321/335/337 and 411/437 | `grep -n "granted_by\|created_by\|source_role_address" endpoints.py` | confirmed at those exact lines |
| `verify_token` returns a constant | `auth.py:91` `return "anonymous"`, `auth.py:102` `return "authenticated"` | confirmed — two constants, no other return path |
| Rejecting the body field would break the only population path | `test_api_endpoints.py:503` / `:608` post it; `schemas.py` marks it required | confirmed |
| Value is durable on both surfaces | `sqlite.py:632` `granted_by TEXT NOT NULL`, `:738` `created_by TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`; `backup.py:102/122`; `context.py:203` | confirmed |

### Claims CORRECTED / EXTENDED

1. **There is a THIRD instance the issue does not name, and it must be treated differently.** `POST /envelopes` takes `defining_role_address` from the body (`endpoints.py:411` region, audit at `:495`) — also an actor claim. But unlike the other two it is **functionally load-bearing**: `engine.py:3232` feeds it to `_compute_envelope_locked(...)` to obtain the parent envelope for the monotonic-tightening check. Marking the *stored* value would make that lookup miss and **silently skip the tightening check**. So its durable value is left untouched and only its audit payload is labelled. This distinction is the reason a uniform "prefix every actor field" fix would have been a security regression.

2. **`granted_by_role_address` carries no functional load; `created_by_role_address` carries a little.** `git grep "granted_by" -- engine.py access.py knowledge.py` returns **empty** (control: the same pattern fires on `clearance.py` and `endpoints.py` in the same invocation, so the instrument is not broken) — it is serialized and never compared. `created_by_role_address` is read once, at `engine.py:3203`, as the `role_address` of the KSP_CREATED audit anchor — a provenance slot, not a decision.

3. **A durable-schema change is BLOCKED, which rules out the "add a `granted_by_claimed` field" spelling of option 2.** `RoleClearance.to_dict()` is pinned by exact string equality to a committed conformance vector: `tests/trust/pact/conformance/test_n6_conformance.py:197` asserts `_canonical_json(clearance.to_dict()) == vector["expected_canonical_json"]` against `vectors/role_clearance.json`. Adding any field changes that string and fails N6. Both sqlite tables also carry fixed columns. So option 2 had to be implemented **in the value, not the shape**.

4. **There is already an in-repo precedent for exactly that.** `yaml_resolvers.py:83` defines `_YAML_ORG_AUTHORITY = "yaml-org-definition"` and writes it into `granted_by_role_address` (`:169`) and `created_by_role_address` (`:202`) for clearances/KSPs materialised from a YAML org definition. The field is already polymorphic — a D/T/R address *or* a provenance marker — and `yaml_resolvers.py:399-400` routes those KSPs through `engine.create_ksp`, so a non-address value already flows through the audit-anchor path in production. ## The class, in one sentence

**A mechanism that learned NOTHING reports the same value as a mechanism that checked and passed.**

The consequence is that correct code and broken code become indistinguishable at the point anyone looks — and the vacuous value is produced exactly when the machinery is misconfigured, which is when a reader most needs the truth.

## The shapes, and why Python makes several of them worse

**1. An empty collection makes a check vacuously pass.**

`all([])` is `True`. That is correct set theory and a dangerous authorization primitive:

```python
if all(perm in user.permissions for perm in required):   # required == [] -> grants
    allow()
```

Three of the sibling's criticals were this shape:
- an auth flow whose `all_passed = True` accumulator was never touched, because the step list was empty — a successful authentication in which zero credential checks ran;
- a `require_all_permissions([])` guard that granted to any caller, while its sibling `require_any_role([])` correctly denied (an asymmetry that made reading one arm tell you nothing about the other);
- a policy object with no rules returning ALLOW, on the reasoning that zero rules vacuously pass.

Note `any([])` is `False`, so the same empty input fails *closed* on one and *open* on the other. That asymmetry is what let these survive review.

**2. A comparison that cannot observe its input.**

`float('nan')` compares `False` against everything, so every bare comparison guard silently admits it:

```python
if temperature <= 0:      # NaN passes. So does inf.
    raise ValueError(...)
```

The high-precision tell: **a function that contains an `isfinite()`/`isnan()` check AND a bare `<`/`>` on a different float.** The guarded operand proves the author knew the hazard and stopped one operand short. In the sibling sweep that single pattern found the known instance plus three more, at near-zero false-positive cost.

Worth checking your JSON boundary specifically: `json.loads('{"x": NaN}')` **accepts** `NaN` by default (`parse_constant`), and `json.loads('1e400')` yields `inf` rather than raising. Both put a non-finite value inside a validator that cannot see it.

**3. A default standing in for an unknown.**

```python
tokens_used = payload.get("tokens_used", 0)     # "not reported" becomes "zero used"
outcome     = payload.get("outcome", "success") # "not reported" becomes "it worked"
```

The tell is a *within-function asymmetry*: the same function usually raises for the fields the author considered load-bearing (`payload["capability"]`) while defaulting the ones they did not. Worth grepping hardest where the value lands in an audit record, a signature/hash pre-image, or a billing figure — there the wrong value is durable and, if signed, harder to challenge later.

**4. A ratio or completeness predicate over an empty basis.**

`0/0` guarded into `1.0`, or `is_complete()` returning `True` because the unexercised list is empty when nothing was ever declared. Reads as "100% covered" from a run that measured nothing.

**5. A gate that counts failures instead of asserting successes.**

```python
if not failures:            # cancelled, skipped, timed-out and never-ran all pass here
    merge()
```

This one bit the sibling's own tooling four times in a single session, most severely when a CI API returned errors: a watcher counting non-successes reported `SETTLED, not-success=NONE` because an empty response yields an empty failure list — byte-identical to a fully green result. The fix is to enumerate required signals **by name** and assert each reported success, plus a non-vacuity guard that refuses when zero signals were observed.

**6. A deferral nothing reads.**

A tracking label or an issue that relies on someone choosing to look is a deletion with provenance. The discriminator is **is there a reader** — a wake-up condition something evaluates, with a date that fails a gate when it passes.

## The part that was hardest to see

One critical had a **test asserting the vulnerability as intended behaviour** — a test literally named for the vacuous outcome, asserting the grant. Anyone checking "is this covered?" found a test, saw green, and moved on.

So `"is it tested?"` is itself an instance of this class. The question that discriminates is `"has this test been shown to fail for the right reason?"` — mutate the mechanism, confirm the test goes red, revert.

## 11474 — `py/weak-sensitive-data-hashing`, `url_credentials.py:731`

> Sensitive data (password) is used in a hashing algorithm (BLAKE2B) that is insecure for password hashing, since it is not a computationally expensive hash function.

### Runtime-safety proof (Rule 1b condition 1)

The rule's premise is **password hashing**: a digest is *stored* and later *matched* to verify a credential, so an attacker who obtains the digest can brute-force the preimage and authenticate. That premise does not hold here, and the guard lines show why.

**1. Authentication completes BEFORE any hashing occurs.** `packages/kailash-mcp/src/kailash_mcp/auth/providers.py:189-204`:

```python
if api_key not in self.keys:              # <- THE auth decision, line 189
    raise AuthenticationError("Invalid API key")

key_data = self.keys[api_key]
...
return {
    "user_id": f"api_key_{fingerprint_secret(api_key)}",   # <- AFTER, opaque id only
```

The fingerprint is not consulted, compared, or persisted for verification. It is a label attached to an already-authenticated request.

**2. No fingerprint anywhere gates an auth decision.** Grepped every `fingerprint ==` / `compare_digest` pairing across `src/` and `packages/`. The only hits are `core/ml/query_patterns.py:358-359` (ML pattern matching), `infrastructure/idempotency_store.py:239` (idempotency replay, comparing a caller-supplied fingerprint, and the file does not import `fingerprint_secret`), `dataflow/performance/migration_optimizer.py:436,559` (schema drift), and a docstring doctest. *Positive control:* the same query finds `compare_digest` in 5 non-test files (`nodes/auth/sso.py`, `mfa.py`, `directory_integration.py`, `enterprise_auth_provider.py`, `delegate/audit.py`), so the query discriminates and the absence is real.

**3. The helper documents the property the rule assumes it is trying to provide, and disclaims it.** `url_credentials.py`, `fingerprint_secret` docstring:

> Fingerprints MUST NOT be treated as secrets. They are derived deterministically from the plaintext with no secret keying material; anyone who knows the plaintext can reproduce the fingerprint. **Do not use fingerprints for access control or verification.**

A slow KDF is also rejected on merit for this call shape: fingerprints are computed on request-rate paths including unauthenticated ones, so a ~10² ms KDF is a CPU-burn amplifier handed to an anonymous caller, in exchange for defeating an offline attack that the high-entropy inputs already defeat.

### SCOPE CAVEAT — read this before citing this dismissal

**This disposition covers the RULE only; the enumerable-input weakness is real and is #2170/#2171.**

The flagged call at line 731 **is** unkeyed:

```
667: def fingerprint_secret(...)              <- line 731 lives HERE, hashlib.blake2b(value...), NO key
740: _PROCESS_KEY_MATERIAL = _secrets.token_bytes(32)
743: def process_local_config_key(...)        <- the KEYED function, a different one
```

and low-entropy inputs genuinely reach it — URLs, filesystem paths, field names, preset names, and a rate-limit identifier that is by its own code comment *"an IP or user id (PII)"*. Against an unkeyed fast hash, a 2^32 IPv4 space is exhaustible. That is a real defect. It is **not** this rule's defect, and it is tracked separately:

- **#2170** — `kaizen/llm/url_safety.py:44` documents its tag as "non-reversible" when it is not (Rule 3e)
- **#2171** — the Nexus rate-limit middleware relies on the fingerprint for a privacy property it does not deliver

Do not read this dismissal as clearance for either.

## 11484 — `gateway/security.py:892`

> This expression logs sensitive data (secret) as clear text. (3 paths)

### Runtime-safety proof

The logged expression is `secrets_dir` — a filesystem **directory path**, defaulting to `/etc/kailash/secrets`. Its only producer is a `str` constructor kwarg:

```python
1010    def __init__(self, secrets_dir: str = "/etc/kailash/secrets", ...):
1018        self.secrets_dir = secrets_dir
1066            _warn_manifest_inside_store(secrets_dir)
```

No secret material joins that path. The master key is a separate variable (`self._master_key`, `:1041`) never interpolated into it, and secret plaintext flows only to `_seal(...)` → `_build_envelope(...)`, never to a logger.

`secrets_dir` occurs in exactly **one file** in the tree (15 occurrences, all in `gateway/security.py`), so all three taint paths must originate at that one constructor parameter. Tests cannot contribute paths — `codeql-config.yml` `paths-ignore` excludes `tests/` and `**/tests/`.

The match is on the **identifier name** `secrets_dir`, not on content. The file already documents this exact mechanism for a sibling case at `:354-357`:

> value — but CodeQL's `py/clear-text-logging-sensitive-data` matches on identifier names, and `SECRET_MANAGER_KEY_ENV` reads as key material to it.

**Why not rename it away:** `secrets_dir` is a public constructor kwarg; renaming is a breaking API change for downstream callers and buys no security.

## Corrections to this issue (both change scope)

**1. The line numbers are stale by exactly +130.** The alerts were raised against commit `4a98750d8cc4d6eca7000818602455cd44b851f3`; on the current tree the same code sat 130 lines lower. Verified against five independent anchors:

**2. The four alerts do NOT share one disposition.** The issue's prose attributes them to the `python_exec` branch. Measured, only **two** are:

| Alert | Branch | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| 131 (`1217`) | `python_exec` | **RESOLVED** by deletion |
| 132 (`1222`) | `python_exec` | **RESOLVED** by deletion |
| 133 (`1231`, now `1275`) | `shell_exec` | **NOT resolved** — keeps its `[<>;&\|`$()]` strip at `1273` |

---

## The real defect (worse than the alerts describe)

The comment `# Remove only the most dangerous HTML tags for XSS prevention` advertised a property the code did not have, by a wide margin. Measured by running the real function:

**Blind to event-handler XSS** — needs none of the four listed tags, returned byte-identical:

```
'<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'  -> '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'
'<svg onload=alert(1)>'         -> '<svg onload=alert(1)>'
'<body onload=alert(1)>'        -> '<body onload=alert(1)>'
```

**Net-negative: it MANUFACTURED the token it existed to remove.** Single-pass `re.sub` lets the fragments either side of a deleted match join:

```
'<scr<script>ipt>'          -> '<script>'
'<scr<script>ipt>alert(1)'  -> '<script>alert(1)'     <-- a live script element
```

So the control synthesized a valid `<script>` element, with executable content, from input that contained no such tag.

**Nesting bypass — CONFIRMED as stated, with a near-miss worth recording.** The issue's literal payload reproduces. But the *closed* variant does not:

```
'<scr<script>ipt>alert(1)</scr</script>ipt>'  -> ''      (correctly stripped)
```

The DOTALL `<script.*?</script>` regex consumes the whole span when a closing tag is present. A test written against the closed form would have **passed for the wrong reason** and certified nothing. Both forms are pinned in the regression test so the distinction survives.

**The branch asymmetry IS the defect.** `shell_exec` strips `[<>;&|`$()]` *before* its script regex; `generic` applies `[<>]` *after*. Both neutralize the fused token (`'<scr<script>ipt>' -> 'scrscriptipt'`). `python_exec` had no angle-bracket strip at any point.

---

## Disposition: the transform is DELETED from `python_exec` (human-authorized)

Removing it beats repairing it: there is no HTML sink for it to protect, escaping there would corrupt the Python data the branch exists to carry, and a transform that manufactures a live tag is worse than absent. `shell_exec` and `generic` are **unchanged except for comments** — their char-class strips already neutralize the fused token, and cutting their removals would change behaviour for the two no-context callers with nothing gained.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] **Answer the question with call-graph evidence** — above; NO, closed 4-caller set.
- [x] **Escape-or-ceremony** — neither was right; the transform is deleted, with the runtime-safety proof below.
- [x] **Nesting bypass addressed** — eliminated by the deletion; both payload forms pinned.
- [x] **Fix the label** — the false "XSS prevention" comment is gone, replaced by a comment stating what the branch does, what it does not, and what to do instead (escape at the sink).

### Runtime-safety proof (zero-tolerance Rule 1b) for alerts 133 / 134, which remain open

Both are **runtime-safe**, each behind a character-class guard that runs unconditionally:

- **Alert 133**, `security.py:1275` — the metacharacter strip at **`security.py:1273`** (`re.sub(r"[<>;&|`$()]", "", value)`) runs **first** and removes `<` and `>` outright, so the flagged regex can never see a tag. It is unreachable *as a tag filter*.
- **Alert 134**, `security.py:1282` — the angle-bracket strip at **`security.py:1289`** (`re.sub(r"[<>]", "", sanitized)`) removes every bracket after the flagged regex runs, so tag injection is denied regardless of what that regex matched. The flagged regex is defence-in-depth behind it.

Verified behaviourally, not by inspection: every event-handler and nesting payload above returns bracket-free from both branches, and `tests/regression/test_issue_2173_sanitize_input_python_exec_not_xss_control.py` pins both guards so a future change cannot quietly remove them.

**Full-fix acceptance criteria** (what closing 133/134 outright would require): replace regex-based tag filtering with a real HTML parser, or route every consumer through sink-side escaping and drop the sanitizer's markup handling entirely. Out of scope here — both branches feed node parameters, not markup.

---

## Related finding: alert 5149 residual — **CLOSED**

The residual check was to confirm `html.escape` is applied at **every** interpolation site in `trust/plane/dashboard.py`. Swept all 75 value slots across 11 markup producers: 74 routed through `_esc`; the exception was `_format_timestamp`, which returned raw text that callers drop straight into markup.

Not exploitable today (every producer coerces via `datetime.fromisoformat`), but that invariant lives in `models.py` / `holds.py` — a cross-file dependency. Now escaped locally on both return paths. Also verified: `_esc` is `html.escape(str(value))` with `quote=True` by default, so attribute breakout is closed; no `<script>`/JSON-in-script contexts exist; `href` values are literal-prefixed. ---

## Reported, deliberately NOT fixed

**1. `javascript:` scheme reassembles on a single pass in ALL THREE branches**, `generic` included:

```

```

The `[<>]` backstop denies tag injection but **not** a scheme landing inside a pre-existing attribute. Lower severity, wider blast radius (every node in the SDK goes through the generic branch) — held for a human call rather than changed unilaterally.

**2. `security.py` audit-log call (`if sanitized != value and config.enable_audit_logging`)** stringifies the **pre-sanitization** value verbatim, truncated at 50 chars, so an attacker-controlled payload goes straight into a log line and truncation can cut mid-sequence. Same class, one function over; left to the corpus-wide log-injection sweep so the two dispositions do not collide.

But the line has a genuine defect of a different class.

## The code

`src/kailash/trust/constraints/commerce.py:149-151`:

```python
logger.info(
    f"Attribution required but no chain provided for beneficiary {beneficiary}"
)
```

with the value taken straight from caller-supplied context at `:114`:

```python
beneficiary = context.get("beneficiary_id")
```

No `validate_id`, no `repr()`, no length bound, no `sanitize_log_value`.

## Impact

- A `beneficiary_id` of `"org-1\nINFO:root:audit: approved"` **forges a second well-formed log record** — the #2040 class.
- A multi-megabyte value drives unbounded log volume.

`kailash.utils.secure_logging.sanitize_log_value` exists for exactly this and its docstring names this call shape:

> Use this wherever a request field -- `user_id`, a tenant id, a header value, a path segment, an email -- is rendered into a log record

guaranteeing the result is *"Single-line and structurally inert"* and *"Bounded"*.

## Secondary consideration for the owner

Emitting a beneficiary identifier at INFO on a **benign** control-flow branch (attribution simply absent) routinely writes a party identifier into logs in a financial-attribution context. Whether that is wanted is a judgement call, flagged rather than assumed.

## Note on CodeQL

Applying `sanitize_log_value` will **not** clear alert 11436, which is the clear-text-logging rule and needs separate false-positive disposition. It does clear the log-injection exposure, and it is recognised as a barrier by the repo's sanitizer model (`.github/codeql/sanitizers/sanitizers.model.yml:86-91`, `LogInjection::ReplaceLineBreaksSanitizer`) because `sanitize_log_value` terminates in `.replace("\r", " ").replace("\n", " ")`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `beneficiary` routed through `sanitize_log_value` before interpolation, with lazy `%s` args rather than an f-string.
- [ ] Sweep the sibling log lines in `commerce.py` for the same shape rather than fixing this one site (`rules/security.md` § Multi-Site Kwarg Plumbing).
- [ ] A regression test asserting on the **emitted stream** — a forged record is forged at format time, so counting `LogRecord`s cannot discriminate.

## Related
- #2040 (the log-injection class), #2106 (the `sanitize_log_value`-as-barrier deferral)

## Confirmed as written

`commerce.py:149-151` and `:114` are accurate — re-derived with `grep -n`, not read off the issue. Both halves of the impact claim were **executed**, not reasoned, against the unfixed code with a `StringIO` handler and a `%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s` formatter:

```
beneficiary_id = "org-1\nINFO:root:audit: approved"
  -> 2 emitted lines, line 2 == "INFO:root:audit: approved"   # a forged record
beneficiary_id = "B" * 5_000_000
  -> 5,000,100 characters emitted
```

After the fix, same inputs: **1** emitted line, **0** lines that start a new record, **229** characters.

## Correction 1 — the barrier is NOT in `sanitizers.model.yml`

The issue attributes the barrier to `.github/codeql/sanitizers/sanitizers.model.yml:86-91`. That file does **not** model this function. Lines 78-93 are a **comment** recording that a `neutralModel` row naming `sanitize_log_value` was tried and **measured ineffective** (PR #2103 analysis at 2026-08-12T04:56Z still reported all four alerts). Its own words: `THE MECHANISM THAT DOES WORK IS IN THE CODE, NOT IN THIS FILE.`

`grep -n sanitize_log_value` on that file returns three hits, all on `#` comment lines.

This matters because anyone tidying that file would believe a barrier lives there. **The barrier claim itself is not stale**: `secure_logging.py` still terminates in `.replace("\r", " ").replace("\n", " ")` as its final returned expression, which is what `LogInjection::ReplaceLineBreaksSanitizer` matches.

## Correction 2 — lazy `%s` is not a barrier

AC-1 asks for `%s` args, which is right, but the reason should be recorded correctly: the record is still formatted at **emit** time, so an unsanitized `%s` argument injects exactly as an f-string does. `sanitize_log_value` is the **entire** defence; `%s` is a cost and style fix. The regression test deliberately does not rely on it.

## Correction 3 — the single-site framing is refuted: 15 sites across 5 files

A single-line `grep` is a blind instrument here (it misses multi-line calls and hits docstrings). An AST sweep for `logger.<level>(...)` calls whose first argument is a `JoinedStr`, fired first at a known-answer case, finds **15** sites in `src/kailash/trust/constraints/`:

| file | sites |
|---|---|
| `commerce.py` | 149 |
| `dimension.py` | 285, 407, 410, 412, 429, 434, 454 |
| `evaluator.py` | 203, 227 |
| `spend_tracker.py` | 167, 237, 294 |
| `builtin.py` | 438, 484 |

All 15 are fixed. `evaluator.py:135` is **not** a site — it is inside a class docstring, which is why the AST instrument and not grep was used.

**Not a uniform patch.** At `builtin.py:484` the value is rendered `{resource!r}`, and `repr()` already escapes newlines — the newline class was closed there. What was missing was the **bound**; a 5 MB `resource_requested` emitted 5,000,137 characters. Sanitizing that site buys length, not escaping.

**Deliberately left unsanitized:** spend amounts and budget totals are numeric by construction (`budget.spent += amount` runs *before* the log call, so a non-numeric amount raises first), and `_validate_resource_path` returns only module-local literals.

## The secondary judgement call — decided: INFO -> DEBUG

The issue flagged this rather than deciding it. **Decision: the record drops to DEBUG.** Reasoning:

1. The branch is **benign** — `check` returns `satisfied=True` whether or not the chain is present — so the record reports no enforcement action.
2. INFO is the default-enabled level in most deployments, so the previous code wrote a financial counterparty identifier into general application logs by default, where retention and access are typically broader than an audit sink's.
3. DEBUG preserves the diagnostic for whoever is actually debugging attribution, which is the only party who needs it.

The alternative — keeping INFO but dropping the identifier — was rejected: it removes the only diagnostic while keeping the log volume. No test pinned the old level (`grep` over `tests/` for the message and for `CommerceConstraint` returns one file, which asserts neither).

Pinned by `test_benign_absent_attribution_does_not_log_the_party_at_info`.

## Separate finding, NOT fixed here

## The code and its own stated intent

`packages/kailash-nexus/src/nexus/auth/rate_limit/middleware.py:182-190`:

```python
# identifier is whatever _identifier_extractor returns -- an IP or
# user id (PII), and by convention sometimes an API key. Log a
# fingerprint so operators can still correlate repeat offenders;
# the raw value stays confined to the rate-limit backend key.
logger.warning(
    "Rate limit exceeded: identifier_fp=%s, path=%s, retry_after=%ds",
    fingerprint_secret(str(identifier)),
    path,
    retry_after,
)
```

The stated goal is that **"the raw value stays confined to the rate-limit backend key"** — i.e. the log gets a correlation tag, not the PII.

## Why the goal is not met

`fingerprint_secret` is unkeyed BLAKE2b truncated to 8 hex chars (`src/kailash/utils/url_credentials.py:730-733`). The default extractor is documented at `:30` and `:99-100` as returning **"user_id from JWT or IP address"**.

For the IP case the input space is 2^32. Against an unkeyed fast hash that is exhaustible in minutes on commodity hardware, so the fingerprint in the log is equivalent to the plaintext IP for anyone who can read the log. The privacy control does not do the job its comment describes.

`fingerprint_secret`'s own docstring is consistent with this and is not the problem — it says plainly:

> Fingerprints MUST NOT be treated as secrets ... anyone who knows the plaintext can reproduce the fingerprint.

The defect is the **call site** relying on a property the helper never claimed.

## Contrast: the keyed helper exists

Three lines below `fingerprint_secret` in the same module:

```python
_PROCESS_KEY_MATERIAL = _secrets.token_bytes(32)

def process_local_config_key(payload: str, *, length: int = 16) -> str:
```

whose docstring states the exact reasoning this call site needs: *"Because the key is secret and random, the derived cache key is not a brute-forceable oracle for the credentials in its pre-image, which a bare digest would be."*

Note the trade-off that makes this a judgement call rather than a mechanical swap: per-process keying breaks **cross-node log correlation**, which `fingerprint_secret` documents as an intentional property. A deployment-wide (not per-process) key preserves correlation while defeating enumeration; that is a design decision, not a one-line change.

## Also worth deciding

The high-entropy cases (an API key as the identifier) are genuinely fine under the current helper. It is specifically the **IP and user-id** cases that are enumerable. A fix may reasonably treat them differently rather than uniformly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide the intended property: correlation-only (then fix the comment, which currently over-promises), or genuine confidentiality (then key the derivation with deployment-scoped material).
- [ ] If keyed: confirm cross-node correlation still works, since that is the stated reason `fingerprint_secret` is unkeyed.
- [ ] Sweep other `fingerprint_secret` call sites whose input is enumerable — measured: `command_safety.py:132` (command), `kaizen/llm/presets.py:79` (preset name), `from_env.py:438` (selector), `url_safety.py:57` (URL), `auth/gcp.py:410,416,421,459` (filesystem path), `dataflow/core/nodes.py:1035` (field name).
- [ ] A test that pins the decision.

`fingerprint_secret` is genuinely unkeyed, and the tag is genuinely reversible:

```
pid=14008 fingerprint_secret('ip:203.0.113.47') = 20b31bf7
recovered='ip:203.0.113.47' after 28976 guesses in 0.224s -> 129,136 guesses/sec
full IPv4 sweep (2**32) at this rate: 9.24 single-core-hours
=== INDEPENDENT SECOND PROCESS ===
pid=16726 fingerprint_secret('ip:203.0.113.47') = 20b31bf7
```

Identical digest across two processes (so no keying of any kind), and the plaintext IP recovered in 0.224 s scanning one /16. Single-core, unoptimised Python, no precomputation.

**Decision on the first acceptance criterion: genuine confidentiality, keyed.** The call-site comment promised the raw value stays out of the log; downgrading to correlation-only would mean accepting that every 429 publishes a client IP to any log reader. The tag is now `HMAC-SHA256(key, DOMAIN || 0x00 || identifier)` truncated to 16 hex. Width doubled from 8 deliberately: 32 bits collides at ~2**16 identifiers by the birthday bound, and a collision merges two offenders under one tag, corrupting exactly the forensic question the tag answers.

**Cross-node correlation is preserved** (second criterion). The key is deployment-scoped via `NEXUS_RATE_LIMIT_FINGERPRINT_KEY`, minimum 32 bytes — the same value on every node yields the same tag for the same client. Per-process keying (the `process_local_config_key` model) would defeat enumeration equally but break correlation, so it is the fallback, not the design. A dedicated variable rather than reusing `NEXUS_JWT_SECRET`, for key separation.

**No key configured is not a silent no-op.** The two properties are dispositioned separately: confidentiality fails **closed** — a random per-process key is minted, so the tag is unforgeable and irreversible with zero operator action — while the degraded property, cross-node/cross-restart correlation, gets a **loud warning at construction** naming the exact variable. There is no fallback to the unkeyed digest and no dropped tag. This mirrors what `auth_bootstrap.build_auth_config` already does for a missing JWT key. A key present but under 32 bytes **raises** at middleware construction rather than being accepted or padded: a short key is worse than none, because the operator believes the control is wired.

**Rate-limit state is unaffected by rotation or restart**, which is the obvious thing to fear and is worth stating explicitly. Buckets are keyed on the raw identifier — `check_and_record(identifier=...)`, and `InMemoryBackend` indexes `self._buckets[identifier]` directly. `grep -rn fingerprint src/kailash/trust/rate_limit/` returns nothing (control grep on the same tree confirms the matcher fires). So a rotation changes emitted tags only: it cannot reset a token bucket, and an attacker cannot wash away an in-progress throttle by provoking one. The cost is that log queries spanning a rotation must be scoped to one key epoch. A regression test pins that no fingerprint reaches the backend.

**Tests pin the property, not the call** (fourth criterion). Asserting "hmac was called" cannot distinguish a real keyed construction from one keyed with a constant, so the suite asserts that different keys disagree on the same identifier and that one key reproduces. Verified by mutation, with the mutation shown to execute: replacing the HMAC with the old unkeyed BLAKE2b reds 3 tests; keeping HMAC but substituting a constant key still reds 2, including `test_different_deployment_keys_produce_different_tags`.

## The false claim

`packages/kailash-kaizen/src/kaizen/llm/url_safety.py:44`:

```python
def _url_fingerprint(raw: str | None) -> str:
    """Produce a short, non-reversible tag for a URL.
```

It delegates to `fingerprint_secret`, which is **unkeyed** BLAKE2b truncated to 8 hex characters (32 bits):

```python
# src/kailash/utils/url_credentials.py:730-733  (function spans 667-733)
digest_bytes = max(1, (length + 1) // 2)
return hashlib.blake2b(value.encode("utf-8"), digest_size=digest_bytes).hexdigest()[
    :length
]
```

A URL is **low-entropy and enumerable**. Against an unkeyed fast hash, anyone holding the logged tag can enumerate candidate URLs and recover the original. "Non-reversible" is false for this input class.

## The canonical helper says so itself

`fingerprint_secret`'s own docstring, same file:

> Fingerprints MUST NOT be treated as secrets. They are derived deterministically from the plaintext with no secret keying material; **anyone who knows the plaintext can reproduce the fingerprint.** Do not use fingerprints for access control or verification.

So the SDK already documents the property correctly in one place and incorrectly in another. That is the `zero-tolerance.md` Rule 3e shape: a doc claim about a code-surface property that does not hold.

## Why it is load-bearing rather than cosmetic

The keyed helper **exists** and is a different function three lines below:

```
667: def fingerprint_secret(...)              <- unkeyed; _url_fingerprint calls THIS
740: _PROCESS_KEY_MATERIAL = _secrets.token_bytes(32)
743: def process_local_config_key(...)        <- keyed; NOT what url_safety uses
```

`process_local_config_key`'s docstring explains exactly why keying matters: *"Because the key is secret and random, the derived cache key is not a brute-forceable oracle for the credentials in its pre-image, which a bare digest would be."*

A reader who trusts "non-reversible" may fingerprint something that genuinely needs to stay secret, and get no protection. The docstring is the interface here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Either correct the docstring to state what the tag actually is (a stable, **enumerable-input-reversible** correlation tag, not a confidentiality control), or switch the call to keyed material if confidentiality is intended — decide which, do not leave both readings available.
- [ ] Sweep the sibling fingerprint docstrings in `kaizen/llm/` (`errors.py:_fingerprint`, `presets.py`, `from_env.py`, `auth/gcp.py`) for the same claim; `url_safety.py` is unlikely to be the only one.
- [ ] A test pinning the corrected claim, so it cannot silently drift back.

## Related
- Alert 11474 (`py/weak-sensitive-data-hashing`) is dispositioned FALSE POSITIVE separately — the rule's store-then-verify premise fails, since no fingerprint gates an auth decision. This issue is the real defect found while checking that.

## 2. The Rule-3e finding stands — with one refinement that changes urgency

"Non-reversible" is false, and the issue is right to call it. But it is false for a narrower input class than the body implies, and the distinction decides how urgent this is.

Measured against merged main:

```
tag for a secret-bearing URL: f85bb659   (32 bits)
recovered from a 12-candidate guess space WITHOUT the api_key: none
```

The credential is **inside the pre-image**. Enumerating scheme + host + path does not recover the tag when a high-entropy key sits in the query string — an attacker must guess the secret too, at which point they already have it.

So precisely:

- **Fully-guessable URL** (`https://metadata.google.internal/`, an internal hostname): recoverable by enumeration. **"Non-reversible" is false here.** This is a *confirmation oracle* — it confirms a guess, it does not reveal an unknown.
- **URL carrying a high-entropy credential**: not recoverable. The credential-disclosure reading of this alert does **not** hold.

That matters because the log line fires on **rejected** endpoints — the guard blocked the request — and the confirmation is available only to someone who can already read the logs.

## 3. Collision behaviour — the cost that is real today

32 bits is a *correlation-quality* limit, and correlation is the only thing the tag exists for:

```
  1,000 distinct rejected URLs -> P(collision) =  0.0%
 10,000                        ->                1.2%
 77,000                        ->               49.9%
200,000                        ->               99.1%
```

## 4. Options

1. **Accept and record.** Cost: nothing changes; the oracle property and the collision ceiling stand.
2. **Key the hash.** Breaks cross-process correlation — the tag's entire purpose — and breaks the log-to-exception join with `errors._fingerprint` unless both key identically, which a per-process key cannot do across services. Not recommended.
3. **Widen to 16 hex (64 bits).** Fixes collisions; does **not** change the oracle property (a guesser confirms either way). Cost: breaks the documented 8-hex cross-SDK contract in `rules/event-payload-classification.md` §2 and every historical log join. Cross-SDK decision, not a patch.

**Recommendation: (1), with the rationale written down rather than inherited.** §2 justifies 8 hex as "insufficient for rainbow-table reversal of typical PK strings" — and a URL is materially more guessable than a random PK, so this call should not silently inherit that sentence. The acceptance worth recording is: *the tag is a confirmation oracle for guessable URLs, that is accepted for the rejected-endpoint log specifically, and 32 bits bounds forensic correlation at roughly 10k distinct rejected URLs per correlation window.*

Whichever way it goes, the word "non-reversible" should come out of both `:83` and `:101` — it is false as written under every option above except (2).

`Endpoint.base_url` routes every URL through `url_safety.check_url()`, which performs a **live DNS lookup** as part of its DNS-rebinding defense. Constructing an `Endpoint` therefore performs network I/O, and fails closed (`InvalidEndpoint: reason=resolution_failed`) whenever the hostname does not resolve.

This issue raises the design question. It does **not** propose a change — the current behaviour may well be correct, and it has security implications either way.

## Evidence

`src/kaizen/llm/deployment.py:129` calls `check_url(v)` inside a Pydantic `field_validator(mode="before")`:

```python
@field_validator("base_url", mode="before")
@classmethod
def _validate_base_url(cls, v: Any) -> Any:
    ...
    check_url(v)
```

`check_url`'s signature offers an opt-out that this call site does not use, and does not expose:

```python
def check_url(url: str, *, resolve_dns: bool = True) -> None:
```

`src/kaizen/llm/url_safety.py:367-371`:

```python
    if not any_resolved and host_lc not in _HTTP_LOCALHOST_ALLOWLIST:
        # Resolution failed entirely — treat as InvalidEndpoint with
        # `resolution_failed`. Caller can retry with resolve_dns=False if the
        # host is intentionally unreachable in the test environment.
        _reject("resolution_failed", url)
```

The comment names an affordance ("caller can retry with `resolve_dns=False`") that **is not reachable through `Endpoint`** — there is no parameter, config field, or context var that plumbs `resolve_dns` from an `Endpoint`/`LlmDeployment` caller down to `check_url`.

## Why this is worth deciding deliberately

1. **Construction is not the moment of egress.** The lookup happens when the object is built, not when a request is sent. A DNS result cached at construction is stale by send time, so the rebinding window it closes is narrow, while the cost (network I/O in a constructor) is paid on every construction.

2. **It makes a validity check depend on ambient network state.** A perfectly well-formed endpoint for a region whose DNS has not yet been published is rejected as invalid. `tests/unit/llm/auth/test_register_bedrock_region.py:104-112` already documents working around exactly this:

   > *"The SSRF guard's DNS resolution check rejects unresolvable hostnames with `resolution_failed`, which is correct behavior — DNS for an unreleased AWS region does NOT resolve until AWS publishes it."*

3. **It is not a complete rebinding defense on its own.** The IP checked at construction and the IP connected to at send time are resolved independently; a rebinding attacker controls the second lookup. Whether the construction-time check adds defense-in-depth or a false sense of coverage is the question.

## Options (not a recommendation)

- **Keep as-is.** Accept construction-time I/O as the cost of the check.
- **Plumb `resolve_dns` through `Endpoint`.** Makes the documented affordance actually reachable; risks callers disabling it in production.
- **Move the resolution check to send time** (in `http_client`), where the resolved IP is the one actually connected to.
- **Enforce at the socket layer** so the checked address and the connected address are the same by construction.

## How this surfaced

`tests/unit/llm/` had a hidden network dependency: fake fixture hostnames split by accident, because `myresource.openai.azure.com` resolves (Azure publishes a wildcard record for `*.openai.azure.com`) while the equally-fake `myfoundry.services.ai.azure.com` does not.

```
myresource.openai.azure.com        RESOLVES        -> 20.89.12.205
myfoundry.services.ai.azure.com    does NOT resolve (gaierror)
```

With `socket.getaddrinfo` stubbed to raise for every host, **255 of 1615** tests under `tests/unit/llm` and **6** under `tests/unit/providers` failed. The test tier has since been made hermetic (see the PR linked below), so this issue is about the production design only — it is not blocking.

### The load-bearing claim was re-derived, not inherited

Per the request in the comment above, "0 additional addresses reach a TCP SYN without it" was measured rather than quoted. Three ladders were compared over 27 hosts with `socket.getaddrinfo` stubbed: `check_url(resolve_dns=True)`, `check_url(resolve_dns=False)`, and `SafeDnsResolver().check_host()`.

The falsifying result was named first: a host where the construction resolve REJECTS, the offline half ACCEPTS, and the connect-time gate ACCEPTS — that host's SYN would newly fire. **Zero such hosts.** Every one of the 11 rebinding cases plus both non-resolving cases is independently rejected at connect time, with the *same* reason bucket (`loopback`, `metadata_service`, `private_ipv4`, `ipv4_mapped`, `link_local`, `resolution_failed`).

The instrument was shown able to print the other answer: run against a deliberately neutered connect gate, the identical harness reports **14** leaks. So the 0 is a discrimination, not a silence.

Answering the three specific questions:

- **(a) Does the connect-time gate re-decide the same thing?** Yes. `_classify_or_raise` calls the same `network_guard` classifiers, and it is invoked from `_SafeHttpTransport.handle_async_request` before `super().handle_async_request`, so the SYN does not fire for a rejected host. `LlmHttpClient` is the only egress path an `Endpoint` has — `client.py` is the sole consumer of `endpoint.base_url` and builds no other client — so there is no route around it.
- **(b) Is the construction-checked address the one connected to?** No, and this is the core of it. They are independently resolved, and *`check_host`'s address is independently resolved from httpx's too*. Dropping the parse-time resolve does not widen that; closing it is option 4's job, and it remains open (below).
- **(c) Is `resolve_dns=False` reachable through `Endpoint`/`LlmDeployment`?** Reproduces exactly. `resolve_dns` occurs in kaizen source only inside `url_safety.py` itself — no parameter, config field, or context var plumbs it. The fix deliberately does not add one: option 2 would make an SSRF knob operator-settable. This stays a call-site decision, so no configuration can turn the DNS half off where it still carries weight, and `check_url`'s own default remains `resolve_dns=True`.

1. **The `url_safety.py:367-371` snippet no longer exists.** On current `main`-derived branches `url_safety.py` is 254 lines and delegates to `kailash.utils.network_guard.check_url`; the `resolution_failed` raise moved there during the #2137/#2150 consolidation. The *substance* of the point still held, which is why the issue is being actioned; only the citation was stale.
2. Path nit: the validator is at `packages/kailash-kaizen/src/kaizen/llm/deployment.py:129`, not `src/kaizen/llm/deployment.py:129`.

### Two findings this surfaced — neither is fixed here

**1. `localhost` is accepted at construction and rejected at connect time.** Parse-time passes `allow_loopback=True, loopback_hosts=_LOOPBACK_LABELS`, so `http://localhost:11434` validates. `SafeDnsResolver.check_host` has **no loopback carve-out at all** and rejects `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` with `reason=loopback`. `ollama_preset` / `lm_studio_preset` / `llama_cpp_preset` / `docker_model_runner_preset` all build a real `Endpoint` inside an `LlmDeployment` that `LlmClient` routes through `LlmHttpClient`, so **local-model deployments construct but cannot send**. This is pre-existing and unrelated to this change (both `resolve_dns` settings behave identically for it), but it is the more serious defect of the two. Deliberately not fixed here: the repair widens an SSRF gate to admit loopback, and landing that inside a diff about removing a redundant lookup is exactly the mistake `d0a60ff29` was reverted for. Note this also means the connect-time gate is *stricter* than the parse-time gate, which independently rules out this change widening anything.

**2. `http_client.py` cites a test that does not exist.** The `LlmHttpClient.__init__` comment claims the single-`httpx.AsyncClient`-construction rule is enforced by `tests/unit/llm/security/test_llm_http_client_uses_safe_dns_resolver.py`. `check_host` resolves, classifies, and then httpx resolves *again* — a check-to-use TOCTOU at the connect boundary. Option 4 (pin the validated address, so the checked address and the connected address are the same by construction) is the real close for DNS rebinding and is untouched by this change; it needs httpx's resolver hook or a pinned-IP connect, which is its own shard. `MiddlewareAccessControlManager.check_session_access` (`src/kailash/middleware/auth/access_control.py:81`) calls `PermissionCheckNode.execute()` with a parameter set that node cannot satisfy. It raises on every call, for every input. Same family as #2108 — an authorization path that can only refuse, shipped as a working feature (`zero-tolerance.md` Rule 2).

**It was unreachable until now**, which is why it never surfaced: `MiddlewareAccessControlManager` was unconstructable because `EnterpriseSecurityEventNode.__init__` asserted on an attribute that did not exist yet. PR #2140 fixed that assert, so this code runs for the first time and fails immediately.

## Measured

Constructing the manager and calling the method:

```
NodeValidationError: Required parameter 'operation' not provided.
Available resolved inputs: ['resource_id', 'cache_level', 'cache_ttl', 'explain',
'include_timing', 'audit', 'strict_validation', 'validate_syntax', 'test_evaluation',
'permission_type', 'check_inheritance', 'include_rules', 'include_hierarchy'].
Mapping suggestions: ['test_evaluation', 'permission_type', 'explain'].
Description: Permission check operation to perform
```

Preceded by the parameter stripping that causes it:

```
[NODE] Unknown parameter(s) for PermissionCheckNode: ['action', 'resource_type', 'user_context'].
Valid parameters: ['audit', 'cache_level', ..., 'operation', 'permission', ..., 'resource_id', ..., 'user_id', ...]
```

Three independent faults in one call:

1. **Three kwargs the node does not declare.** `user_context=`, `resource_type=` and `action=` are all stripped by `Node.execute` before `run()` sees them, so the call arrives with only `resource_id`.
2. **The one required parameter is not passed.** `PermissionCheckNode.get_parameters()` marks exactly one parameter required — `operation` — and the call site never sets it. Verified:
   ```
   required: ['operation']
     declared(user_context) = False
     declared(resource_type) = False
     declared(action)        = False
   ```
3. **The return shape is misread.** `_check_permission` returns `{"result": {"allowed": ..., "reason": ...}}` (`permission_check.py:481`), while the caller reads `result.get("allowed", False)` at the top level. Even with 1 and 2 fixed, every decision would evaluate to `allowed=False` — a fail-closed accident, not a check.

## Sibling — sweep with it

`check_workflow_access`'s audit call (`access_control.py:129`) is the same shape and also always raises:

```python
self.audit_node.execute(
    event_type="workflow_access_check",   # not declared
    user_id=user_context.user_id,         # declared
    resource_id=workflow_id,              # not declared
    permission=permission.value,          # not declared
    allowed=decision.allowed,             # not declared
    reason=decision.reason,               # not declared
)
```

`EnterpriseAuditLogNode` requires `operation` (not passed) and declares only `user_id` of the six. Every other `execute()` call site in this module should be swept in the same change rather than fixed one at a time — per-site fixes here are exactly the drift `security.md` § Multi-Site Kwarg Plumbing describes.

## Why PR #2140 did not fix it

Deliberate stop, not an oversight. The correct call needs a `permission=` string (`f"session:{action}"`? `"session.access"`? something the admin schema already uses), and choosing that convention is an **authorization-schema decision**, not a mechanical repair. Guessing it would replace a loud failure with a silently *wrong* authorization check — strictly worse than the current state.
